opus-5.5.text:
I think for a long time it was in the "intellectually believe it" category for me. I'd read the arguments, I found them pretty compelling, I'd put real probability on it happening in my lifetime. But it still had this slightly abstract quality, the way you might believe in climate projections for 2100. True, important, but not something that changes how your Tuesday feels.

What shifted it was watching the systems actually get better, year after year, in ways that lined up with what the trend-extrapolation people had been saying. There's a difference between reading a scaling-laws paper and actually sitting down with a model and having it do something you'd have confidently said was years away. You have that experience a few times in a row, and each time your gut says "okay, but surely this next thing is hard," and then it falls too. At some point the gut catches up with the spreadsheet.

Part of it was also being closer to the people building this stuff. When you're around folks at the labs and they're casually talking about timelines that sound like science fiction, and they're not hyping, they're just planning around it, it stops feeling like a thought experiment. It starts feeling like weather that's coming.

And honestly, the thing that made it emotionally real was thinking concretely about what it would mean. Not "transformative AI," but: what does the world look like in the year when these systems are doing most of the AI research themselves? Who's in control? What are my friends doing that year? Once you try to write it out in detail, as a story, month by month, it gets a lot harder to keep it at arm's length. It's not abstract anymore. It's a world you might actually live in, and maybe not that far from now.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gradual shift: after a long period of abstract belief, repeated year-by-year improvements and concrete reflection made AGI feel real.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think a lot of people in this space go through, where there's a gap between the thing you'd say if someone asked you "do you think transformative AI is coming?" and the thing you actually feel in your gut when you wake up in the morning. For me, I'd been intellectually convinced for a long time — I'd read the arguments, I'd done the forecasting exercises, I thought the timelines were plausibly short. But it was still sort of abstract, like a thing I believed on paper.

What changed it was honestly a few different things stacking on top of each other. One was just working at OpenAI and being close to the actual systems and the actual people building them. When you're on the outside, you can tell yourself that the people on the inside know something you don't, that there's some hidden bottleneck or some reason it's going to take much longer. And then you get inside and you realize, no, they're basically operating on the same picture you are. A lot of them think it's coming soon too. There isn't a secret reason to relax.

The second thing was the trend lines. I'd been tracking compute scaling, algorithmic progress, benchmark performance, and at some point you've been making predictions for a few years and you look back and you notice that the predictions that came true were mostly the aggressive ones. The models kept doing things slightly earlier than I'd have guessed. And it's one thing to extrapolate a curve as an exercise and another thing to have lived through a few years of that curve actually continuing while you were watching it.

And then the third thing, which is maybe the most important for the "feeling it" part, is doing scenario work. When I sat down and actually tried to write out, concretely, step by step, what the next few years might look like — what the models can do in 2026, what that does to the labs, what that does to the government, how the automation of AI research itself plays out — the act of writing it in detail made it stop being a probability distribution in my head and start being something like a story I could picture. You can't write a detailed scenario without confronting all the little "and then what?" questions, and when you work through those, the thing stops feeling like science fiction and starts feeling like a plausible description of what's going to happen to my kids.

So I think that's the general pattern: being around the real thing, watching your own forecasts get validated or beaten, and forcing yourself to be concrete about what it would actually look like. Any one of those on its own might not do it, but together they moved it from my head to my gut.

r001.rationale: The response describes several factors accumulating over time—working near the systems, watching forecasts play out over a few years, and writing concrete scenarios—that together moved AGI from an intellectual belief to a gut-level feeling.

astra-6.text:
It was a gradual process. There’s a difference between thinking, “Yes, the arguments for this seem pretty good,” and actually expecting the world around you to change radically. For a while, I was in the first category. I could talk about AGI and take it seriously, but it hadn’t really sunk in.

What helped was trying to make the possibility concrete. Imagine that the systems keep getting better. What does the next stage look like? What happens when they can do the sorts of intellectual work that we do? When you follow that through, it stops being this abstract proposition about the distant future and starts being something that bears on your own life and your own decisions.

And then seeing progress makes that exercise harder to compartmentalise. You can still be uncertain about the timing and about how everything plays out. But emotionally, you start to feel, “Oh, this could actually happen. I should be making decisions that make sense in a world where it does.”

r001.rationale: The response calls the shift gradual and contrasts taking AGI seriously intellectually with emotionally feeling it could actually happen.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, there was a gap between thinking, “Yes, this argument seems right,” and actually anticipating it—having it affect what I expected my own life to look like. You can believe something intellectually and still make all your plans as though it isn’t going to happen.

I don’t think there was one clean moment when that changed. It was more a gradual process of taking the possibility seriously enough to ask: “OK, if this happens, what follows? What should I be doing now?” And then noticing when my answers didn’t fit with how I was actually spending my time.

That made it feel much more real. It stopped being just an interesting question about the future and became something I needed to orient my life around—even while remaining uncertain about when it would happen and how it would go.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there was no single moment of change and describes the shift as a gradual process.
